doc.title: Bill Mays interviewed by Monk Rowe, via Zoom, December 5, 2025

title: Blindfold test: New York State of Mind and working with singers on commissions
summary: He discusses his WDR Big Band commission, then arranging for Mark Murphy, Ann Hampton Callaway and Morgana King, where he ended up singing a verse.

blocks.x: All right. Let me try this one.

Yeah that’s “Sunday in New York” and it was part of a – I was commissioned to write a program that I decided we would call “New York State of Mind” for the WDR Big Band in Cologne. And it was about ten years ago. And we also did that program with the U.S. Air Force Airmen of Note. And the project included Marvin Stamm, my wonderful friend and great trumpet player. And Marvin and I were the featured soloists, along with soloists in the band on that project.
When you get a commission do you prefer that you be wide open to decide what to do or do you prefer some guidance? I mean what kind of guidance comes with a commission?

Yeah I love both. I love being complet – in this instance there were no parameters given except, “We want you and Marvin to come and be the soloists. You pick the material, you title the production.” So that was completely wide open. I chose tunes that were related to “52nd Street Theme,” “Broadway Boogie” by Ornette Coleman, “All Across the City” Jim Hall, “There’s a Boat Leaving Soon for New York” etcetera, etcetera, and I wrote an original called “Manhattan Soliloquy.” But then there are projects like, well when I worked with Mark Murphy or when I worked with Ann Hampton Callaway as an arranger for their records. They would sit at my elbow and hum a line and say, “I’d like this to be the intro, make something of that.” Or they’d have very specific suggestions about the form of the arrangement. And I enjoyed that as well. It took some of the pressure off to have their input and their direction. So I like working either way. Another contrast I did an album for Morgana King called “Simply Eloquent” and she gave me the list of tunes in her keys and said, “Just be Bill Mays and do what you want and send me the stuff in advance.” So I did all the charts and did a mock-up, this was before synthesizers, a piano mock-up and sent her material, and she learned it and came to the date. Now that gave rise to an interesting incident. She hadn’t learned the verse to Gershwin’s “Let’s Call the Whole Thing Off.” So she was having a little problem with it. We’re in the studio, the clock is ticking and the band is waiting. And I’m singing her the

verse trying to teach it to her and she says, “Well you sound great, you sing it.” And I said, “What are you talking about, it’s your date?” She said, “Roll the tape, you sing it.” So I did and I ended up on the record, I think it was the first time I’d ever sung on anybody’s album. And then that opened a Pandora’s box, you can’t shut me up. I love to sing and I’ve sung on several of my recordings since. For better or for worse.
